html:
Long read7 min left

The quiet economics of latency

A checkout that answers in 90 milliseconds and one that answers in 400 look identical in a screenshot. They do not look identical in a revenue report.

The teams that win here are rarely the ones with the fastest servers. They are the ones who measured the ninety-fifth percentile instead of the mean, and then went looking for the tail.

Tail latency is where the money hides. A median of 120ms with a p95 of two seconds means one in twenty sessions is quietly being taught that your product is unreliable.

The fix is almost never a rewrite. It is a cache with a sane eviction policy, a query that stopped fanning out, a payload that shed the fields nobody rendered.

Budget latency the way you budget cost. Give every screen a number, publish it, and let a failing build be the thing that tells you the number moved.

Do that for two quarters and the graph stops being a graph. It becomes a habit, and habits are the only performance work that survives a reorg.

Ilona Petrov · Platform weekly

html:
Chapter 1 of 5Origins

01 · Origins

Before the dashboard there was the ledger, and before the ledger there was a person who wanted to remember what happened on Tuesday.

Counting is older than writing. The tally is the first interface, and every chart you will ever ship is an argument with that tally about what deserves to be remembered.

02 · Scale

A number becomes a shape the moment you decide what a pixel is worth. That decision is design, not maths.

Choose a baseline and you have chosen a conclusion. The honest move is to show the baseline, not to hide it under a gradient.

03 · Colour

Hue carries meaning long before the legend is read, which is why a red bar is never neutral.

Encode order with lightness, category with hue, and nothing at all with saturation unless you enjoy being misread.

04 · Time

Everything measured is measured against a clock somebody chose. Weekly aggregation is an opinion about what a week means.

When the axis is time, the reader is looking for a turn. Give them the turn, annotate it, and stop pretending the data speaks.

05 · Doubt

The last chapter is the one most decks skip: the part where you say how wrong the number could be.

An interval drawn honestly buys more trust than three decimal places ever will.

rfc-041.md0%

RFC 041 — Offline write queue

This document proposes a durable client-side queue so that composing, editing and deleting continue to work when the network does not. It replaces the ad-hoc retry logic currently duplicated in four screens.

Motivation

Roughly nine percent of sessions in the field report at least one failed mutation. Users retry by hand, which produces duplicates that support then has to merge.

queue.push({ op: 'note.update', id, patch, at: now() })

A single queue gives us ordering, deduplication by operation key, and one place to express conflict policy instead of four.

Design

Operations are appended with a monotonic clock and flushed in order. A flush that fails with a retryable status backs off; a flush that fails with a conflict hands the operation to the merge resolver.

Ordering is the contract. Everything else is an optimisation.

The resolver is per entity type and ships with the entity, so a new model cannot enter the system without declaring how it merges.

Risks

A long-lived queue can hold stale intent. We expire operations after seven days and surface the discard to the user rather than dropping it silently.

Storage pressure on low-end devices is bounded by a soft cap of five hundred operations, past which the oldest non-critical entries are trimmed.

Sorting complaints by heat

The brief asked for a redesign. What the team actually needed was a decision about who the product was for, and nobody had written that down in two years.

So we started with the support inbox instead of the canvas. Four hundred threads, tagged by hand over three days, sorted by how angry the sentence sounded.

Two clusters emerged. People who lived in the tool every day wanted density and shortcuts. People who visited twice a month wanted to be told what to do next.

You cannot serve both with one default. You can serve both with one layout and two entry points, which is cheaper than it sounds and far cheaper than a second app.

The daily driver gets a command palette and a table that remembers its columns. The visitor gets a checklist that disappears the moment it stops being useful.

Six weeks later the angry sentences had moved. They were now about export formats, which is the sound of a product that has stopped being confusing and started being used.

That is the whole method. Read the complaints, sort them by heat, and let the second-loudest group tell you what to build after you have calmed the first.

Step 1 of 4Create the workspace

Create the workspace

Pick a workspace name and an owner. Everything else is reversible, including the name, so do not spend the afternoon on it.

Owners can transfer the workspace later without support involvement. Billing follows the owner unless a separate billing contact is set.

Bring your data across

Point the importer at a CSV or connect the source directly. The first pass is a dry run and shows you exactly what will be created.

Rows that fail validation are downloadable with the reason attached, so a fix is an edit and a re-upload rather than a support thread.

Add the team

Invite by email or share a join link scoped to a role. Links expire after seven days and can be revoked at any time.

Roles are additive. A viewer promoted to editor keeps their saved views and filters instead of starting from an empty screen.

Turn it on

Flip the workspace to live and the sandbox data is archived rather than deleted. You can restore it for thirty days.

The launch checklist stays available under settings, so the parts you skipped remain visible until you dismiss them on purpose.

html:
1 · Audit the callers

List every service that reads the orders table directly. Nine of them do; four have no owner listed in the registry, so start by finding one.

Nothing moves until the list is closed. A migration with an unknown reader is a migration with an unknown rollback.

2 · Dual write

Writes go to both stores behind one transaction boundary. The new store is not read yet, so a failure there degrades to a logged alert rather than a 500.

Let it soak for a week and compare row counts nightly.

3 · Backfill

Copy history in ascending id batches of five thousand, checkpointing after each batch so an interrupted run resumes instead of restarting.

Throttle against replica lag, not against wall clock.

4 · Cut over reads

Flip reads behind a percentage flag: one percent, ten, fifty, then all. Compare checksums on the shadow path before each bump.

Keep the flag for a full release cycle. Reverting a flag is cheaper than reverting a deploy.

5 · Drop the old path

Delete the dual write, then the old table, then the code that knew about it. Leave the shim in place for one more release with a loud deprecation log.

The migration is finished when the old name no longer appears in the repository.

html:
HandbookOverview

Overview

This handbook describes how the platform team works: what we own, how work reaches us, and what you can expect when you ask for something.

Ownership

We own the build pipeline, the deploy path, the shared runtime image and the incident tooling. We do not own product services, and we will not merge a change into one on your behalf.

Anything with a name in the registry has a rota. Anything without one is, by definition, ours until an owner claims it.

Intake

Requests arrive in one queue. There is no side channel, and a direct message is not an escalation path, it is a message that will be answered slower than a ticket.

Urgent means someone is currently unable to ship. Everything else is scheduled.

On call

One primary, one shadow, weekly handover on Wednesday so the weekend is never someone's first day. The shadow answers nothing alone.

Pages that fire twice without action get their alert deleted or their threshold changed, in the same week.

Reviews

Two approvals for anything touching the deploy path, one for everything else. A review older than three days is a review that gets a nudge, not a bypass.

Time off

Book it, note it in the rota, hand over the pager. Nobody carries the pager on leave, and no exception has ever been worth the cost.

html:
%
read0 / 612 words

Against the estimate

Every team I have worked on has, at some point, tried to fix estimation. They tried points, then hours, then t-shirts, then points again with a different name.

None of it worked, because the problem was never the unit. The problem is that an estimate is a forecast produced by the one group with the strongest incentive to be optimistic.

What does work is slicing. A task nobody can describe in two sentences is not a task, it is a wish, and a wish has no duration.

Cut until each piece is boring. Boring pieces are predictable, and a stack of predictable pieces is the only honest schedule anyone has ever shipped.

The second thing that works is counting. Not estimating, counting: how many pieces of this size did we actually finish in the last six weeks? That number is not a promise, it is evidence, and evidence survives contact with a stakeholder in a way a promise does not.

You will still be wrong. You will be wrong by a factor that stays roughly constant, which means you can plan around it. Being reliably wrong is a superpower; being unpredictably right is not a plan.

Notebook, week 34

html:
i

The Vanishing Ledger

A short account of the Bell Street accounts office, and of the nine weeks in which its books recorded nothing at all.

M. Adeyemi

ii

The office kept two ledgers, which was ordinary, and reconciled them monthly, which was not. Everyone agreed the practice had begun under Halloran, and nobody could say when Halloran had left.

iii

The first missing week was noticed by a clerk who had been looking for something else entirely. She wrote a note, filed it correctly, and heard nothing for a month.

iv

By the time the second ledger was requested, it had been archived. By the time it was retrieved from the archive, the request had expired and had to be made again, in writing, by someone senior.

v

What the auditors eventually found was not fraud. It was a procedure that had continued for eleven years after the reason for it had been forgotten, and had quietly stopped working in the third.

vi

The recommendation ran to a single line: write down why, next to what. The office adopted it, and the ledgers have balanced ever since.

End

html:
01ArrivalReykjavik, 04:10

The plane lands in a light that has no hour attached to it. Nobody on board can agree whether it is very late or very early, and the terminal has decided not to say.

Two hundred kilometres of black rock with a white line down the middle. The radio finds one station and holds it like a rope.

The ground here breathes. You can stand close enough to feel it on your face and still be told, politely, by a small sign, to stand further back.

A single wire runs for eleven kilometres with no gate and no animals on either side of it. Someone built it. Someone maintains it.

Night arrives like a decision rather than a process. The tent is loud for an hour, then the wind drops and it is the quietest place any of us have been.

The same light again, at the other end. You cannot photograph it, which is why everyone is standing at the window trying.
